stories.title: Diplomacy over reopening the Strait of Hormuz

claims.text: Iran's President Pezeshkian said Iran and Oman will sign an agreement Monday in Muscat on a joint shipping route through the Strait of Hormuz, in the presence of Arab Gulf foreign ministers, with the IMO then notified.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters no signed agreement is expected from Monday's Muscat meeting, saying Iran still wants to collect transit fees from ships using the strait, which Oman rejects.
Bahrain said it will not attend the Muscat meeting or any collective meeting involving Iran until diplomatic relations are restored (ties cut in January 2016).
Pezeshkian said Iran will reopen the Strait of Hormuz when the United States ends its naval blockade and attacks, adding Washington failed militarily and turned to economic pressure.

Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency said the Iran-Oman shipping route agreement will be presented at Monday's Muscat meeting, which Iraq will also attend, but the strait will not reopen unless seven Iranian conditions conveyed to the U.S. are met.
Ebrahim Azizi, head of Iran's parliament national security committee, wrote on X that 'as long as the American side does not accept all of Iran's conditions, dialogue and negotiation are of no use.'
Iran's president Pezeshkian met Egypt's president amid rising regional tensions.
Pezeshkian wrote in a U.S.-aimed social media post: 'Our people can't be bullied into submission. Iran won't surrender.'

Oman's Foreign Minister Badr Albusaidi posted late Sunday that Monday's regional meeting between Iran and Gulf Arab states on Strait of Hormuz navigation was postponed 'in the interests of consensus.'

CNN reported the Hormuz meeting had been set for Monday in Salalah and is now indefinitely postponed, with Saudi Arabia having submitted amendments over concerns the draft framework could lock in a new status quo unacceptable to the Gulf states.

Iran's Fars news agency cited a foreign ministry official saying the postponement came at the request of some regional countries in a decision jointly made by Tehran and Muscat, and that Iran will coordinate with Oman on a new date.
A US official said 'Iran does not control the Strait of Hormuz and never will.'
Three sources told CNN the Trump administration wants to refocus any future US-Iran negotiations on Tehran's nuclear program rather than on reopening the strait.
Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told Al-Arabi Al-Jadeed that Iran will not reopen the strait until the United States satisfies Tehran's demands, regardless of any agreement with Oman.
Oman announced the Monday Iran-Gulf meeting on reopening the Strait of Hormuz was postponed; Iran said the postponement came at Saudi Arabia's request.
Trump on Monday repeated his claim that Iran wants to make a deal quickly.
Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, wrote on X: 'No talks until Iran's conditions are met.'
The IRGC Navy declared Monday: 'The Strait of Hormuz is closed and still under our smart control.'
Secretary of State Marco Rubio called Oman's foreign minister Tuesday to discuss de-escalation and reopening Hormuz, per the State Department.

China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi met his Iranian counterpart Abbas Araghchi in Beijing on September 16, urging the US and Iran to show restraint, return to the Islamabad memorandum, and hold substantive consultations.
Wang Yi pressed specifically for reopening the Strait of Hormuz and for preventing the conflict from spilling into Yemen and the Red Sea.
Reuters notes China is Iran's main oil buyer, so a closed Strait of Hormuz also hurts Beijing.
Treasury Secretary Bessent said the expected Trump-Xi meeting will cover Iran and China's financial links to Tehran.
Japan's Kyodo News reported that Iran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within seven days if the United States takes steps toward easing military pressure.

U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held a roughly three-hour meeting (about 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. ET) with Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi on the UNGA sidelines, mediated by Qatar — the first known high-level contact since the ceasefire and memorandum of under
Trump called the Tuesday meeting 'a very good meeting, very productive' and said another meeting is 'scheduled in the very near future'; Witkoff said he feels 'very good' about it.

The format of the Tuesday meeting is contested: the New York Times, citing two Iranian officials, reports Araghchi met Witkoff and Kushner directly, while Trump later clarified they met 'with mediators of Iran, merely mediators' — the format is unresolved.
Iranian media said the Tuesday meeting came at Washington's request and centered on Tehran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz; the U.S. side has not verified this account.
A senior Iranian official told Reuters the Hormuz proposal was conveyed via mediators on September 16 and that Iran's UNGA delegation has 'full authority' to revive diplomacy.
The senior Iranian official told Reuters that President Pezeshkian will NOT meet Trump in New York, even as Rubio said Trump remains open to a meeting.

Iranian state media reported Tehran's conditions for reopening Hormuz as: immediate lifting of the naval blockade, release of frozen Iranian funds, and an end to the war across all 'resistance' fronts — but IRGC-linked Iranian media denied Tehran adopted any new position, and the

In a late-Tuesday X post, Steve Witkoff said the U.S. and Iran 'engaged in lengthy talks on Tuesday' via mediators 'who shuttled between the two sides throughout the day,' a round he hopes 'will prove constructive and promising,' and that the mediators will continue their work.
The White House clarified that Trump did not attend Monday's three-hour UNGA meeting — the U.S. side was Witkoff and Kushner — after Trump's initial comments created confusion about who participated.
An Iranian security source told Al Jazeera there could be room for further engagement between the U.S. and Iran if Washington meets Tehran's conditions.

stories.title: Drone attack shuts Saudi East-West pipeline

claims.text: President Trump told reporters in Dublin that Iran was 'probably' behind the Thursday drone attack launched from Iraq that shut Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline (~5 mb/d to the Red Sea).

Trump said Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman called him twice Thursday urging U.S. strikes on the Houthis as they advanced in Yemen; Trump declined, saying the U.S. is focused on freedom of navigation.

Trump said the Houthis called his administration saying they do not want the U.S. directly involved; the Islamic Resistance in Iraq denied responsibility for the pipeline attack, and Iraq closed some borders as a precaution.
Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline remained shut on Sunday as a precaution after Thursday's drone attack; the 1,200-km line had been moving 4-5 million barrels per day, about 5% of global supply.
Satellite images showed black smoke south of Medina near the East-West pipeline after the drone attack, and some injuries were reported.
Iraq dismissed a military commander on Saturday after Baghdad and Riyadh both said the pipeline drone attack had originated in Iraq, where Iranian-backed militias operate.

The East-West pipeline stayed closed all weekend; traders and Saudi buyers say Riyadh has enough oil stored at its Red Sea port of Yanbu for just five to seven days if it stays shut, after which as much as 4% of global supply could be jeopardized; repair estimates range from days

Traders said a prolonged shutdown of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline could 'cut off as much as 4% of global oil supply' while the strait is largely blockaded; Riyadh has not said when operations resume.
Saudi Arabia hopes to resume partial operations on the East-West Pipeline within days, but damaged pumping stations could take six to eight weeks to fully repair.
The 750-mile East-West line can carry up to 7 million barrels a day to Yanbu on the Red Sea, bypassing Hormuz.
Rystad's Janiv Shah estimates Yanbu's stored crude covers roughly three days of exports, with another week possible by drawing on crude stored in Egypt.
LSEG data show Yanbu loadings fell to 1.1M bpd in August versus 4M+ bpd in April-June, as Houthi Red Sea attacks deterred traffic.

Shipping sources say Saudi Arabia has suspended oil loadings at the port of Yanbu on the Red Sea, the terminus of the East-West pipeline; full repair of the pumping stations is still seen at six to eight weeks.
The Saudi East-West pipeline still needs six to eight weeks for full repair, with oil loadings at Yanbu remaining suspended.
The Associated Press put the East-West pipeline repair at three to five weeks, shorter than the six-to-eight-week figure reported earlier by Reuters.
Saudi Arabia blamed an Iraq-based pro-Iranian movement for the Friday attack that knocked out the East-West Pipeline across the Arabian desert.

MUFG, cited by the Wall Street Journal, says Saudi Arabia aims to restore about half of the East-West pipeline's capacity within days and a full return within six weeks; ICIS estimates 2 to 2.5 million barrels per day could come back quickly.
Saudi Arabia's energy ministry confirmed technical teams are on site assessing the damaged East-West pipeline.
Three East-West Pipeline pumping stations were damaged — one more than previously assessed — yet the market took it in stride.

Saudi Arabia restarted operations at its East-West Pipeline at a low pumping rate and could resume crude exports from the Red Sea port of Yanbu later on Tuesday, per three sources briefed on the matter; drone attacks forced the shutdown on September 13.

Around 2.4 million barrels a day of Saudi crude and condensate flowed through the Strait of Hormuz over the past two weeks, returning to levels last seen in early July, per Kpler; the four-week average of Saudi crude loadings from inside the Persian Gulf rose above 2 million barr

stories.title: Houthi west-coast offensive / govt counter-offensive around Mokha

claims.text: Yemeni government forces announced they will deploy weapons and aircraft to retake areas seized in the Houthi lightning offensive, including the road to the port city of Mokha.
Satellite and open-source imagery show the Houthis mobilizing on Sept 12, days after capturing Mokha, Perim Island, Dhubab and the Hanish islands.
An adviser to Iran's supreme leader called the Houthi west-coast advance a 'clear victory' in a post on X.
Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed a large-scale missile-and-drone strike on a Saudi military base in Sharurah in southern Saudi Arabia, targeting weapons depots and command-and-control centers.
The Houthis said the Sharurah strike answered a wave of Saudi airstrikes they put at 129 sorties over 48 hours, a count Saudi Arabia had not confirmed.
Saudi Civil Defence said a Houthi projectile injured two people in the Jazan region and damaged several buildings, including a mosque.
Yemeni government forces said they struck Houthi positions in Mokha on Saturday and carried out three airstrikes in the Taiz region on Sunday.
The Yemeni military said it launched airstrikes Sunday on Houthi positions in Mokha, the coastal town of Dhubab, and elsewhere in Taiz province.
The Houthis reported Saudi/Saudi-backed strikes Sunday afternoon on Saada and artillery shelling in the Monabbih border district; the claims are unverified.

A government-allied force (the National Resistance) claimed more than 500 government fighters have been killed on the west coast over the past four weeks and about 1,500 wounded since Aug. 9, while claiming 1,000+ Houthis killed in Hodeida and Taiz; the claims are unverified.

Yemen presidential council member Sultan al-Arada called the collapse of government forces in Mokha 'painful and regrettable' and said forces are regrouping and will 'return to the battle in one form or another.'
Saudi jets pounded Houthi positions around Mokha ahead of a planned counter-offensive by government loyalists; government forces rallied south of the city, regaining some territory.
The Houthis dispersed fighters through Mokha and are fortifying coastal positions; they also launched a new offensive east to cut off Taiz and besiege the government-held city.
Presidential council head Rashad Alimi dismissed the setback as 'incidental' and vowed the government would reclaim sovereignty over all national territories.
The UN estimates more than 80,000 people have been displaced by the fighting since the start of September.
Saudi Civil Defense lifted danger alerts Monday for Najran, Khamis Mushait, Jazan, and Abha amid the recent Houthi attack uptick.

The Houthis said Monday they fired dozens of missiles and drones at a military airbase in Khamis Mushait in southern Saudi Arabia, targeting hangars, radar systems, runways and ammunition depots, in retaliation for Saudi airstrikes in Yemen.
Saudi authorities re-issued emergency alerts in Khamis Mushait and three other southern cities, reversing Monday morning's lifting of those alerts.
The Saudi-led coalition said 13 civilians were wounded in the Khamis Mushait strike.

Saudi and Yemeni air forces stepped up bombardment of Houthi targets including around Mokha, but the Houthis kept 'effective control over almost the entire western coast' of Yemen along the Red Sea and are digging in.
Three sources told Reuters Washington has so far resisted Saudi requests for direct military intervention beyond intelligence support.
Trump said over the weekend he had spoken with the Saudi crown prince, and that the Houthis had also contacted Washington urging it to stay out of the fight.
Saudi state media reported Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman met US regional commander Admiral Brad Cooper in Jeddah on Monday.

Reuters reports the Houthis launched 'a new wave of attacks on Saudi Arabia' and are digging into positions on Yemen's western Red Sea coast, while 'urgent deliberations' are underway in Riyadh over how to respond.
Saudi and Yemeni air forces stepped up bombardment around Mokha, but the Houthis 'maintained effective control over almost the entire western coast,' per Yemeni officials.
Houthi media reported capturing Saudi-recruited fighters on the Hanish Islands, about 160 km north of Bab el-Mandeb — a Houthi-media claim, not independently verified.
Analyst Mohammed Al-Basha: 'All signs now point to a large-scale Saudi retaliation, and that likelihood is increasing by the day.'

Abdulmalik al-Houthi's 350,000-strong force moved weapons and thousands of troops around Mokha in mid-August, then used control of Yemeni telecoms to intercept enemies' calls and sow confusion during the seizure of Perim Island.
Cambridge's Elisabeth Kendall: 'They feel they've won the civil war... they aren't afraid of the United States.'
UNHCR says at least 80,000 people have been displaced by escalating Yemen fighting in recent days.
The IOM puts displacement at 82,000-plus since September 1, including more than 2,000 who fled across the Gulf of Aden to Djibouti.
A Houthi official said Tuesday that Saudi warplanes struck Yemen, killing three people including two children — a Houthi claim with no independent verification.
The IOM now reports nearly 94,000 people displaced in southwestern Yemen (up from 80-82,000 this morning), with 2,000+ crossing to Djibouti — not yet approved-outlet verified.
Reuters profiled Abdul Malik al-Houthi's sweep along Yemen's Red Sea coastline, seizing Mocha and Perim Island at Bab el-Mandeb, as his biggest military victory in years.

Reuters reports al-Houthi built a force of tens of thousands armed with drones and ballistic missiles that withstood years of Saudi-led airstrikes, making him Iran's most prominent and resilient Arab ally after the killings of Hezbollah and Hamas leaders.
Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree declared on September 13 that continued Saudi operations would be met with more severe and larger operations deep inside Saudi territory.
The US stepped up intelligence and targeting support for the Saudi campaign in Yemen with tight limits: no direct strikes and no refueling.
The UN refugee agency reports around 80,000 people have been displaced in recent days by fighting along Yemen's Red Sea coast.

Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed fresh drone and missile strikes on the Red Sea oil port of Yanbu and on the Khamis Mushait airbase, without saying when; Riyadh has confirmed neither side's claims.

Saree said Saudi forces carried out as many as 450 airstrikes on Yemen this week, while Saudi-backed government officials acknowledged their forces and Saudi Arabia were conducting airstrikes on Houthi positions.
The Houthis released battlefield video showing fighters seizing armoured vehicles from Saudi-backed forces amid overhead warplanes and explosions.

A Yemeni living in Saudi Arabia was killed Thursday in Taif when Saudi air defenses intercepted a Houthi-launched drone; a Saudi woman and a Pakistani resident were injured, the first death Riyadh has announced this month.
Saudi officials say 86 people have been injured in Houthi attacks this month.
The Houthis did not claim any attacks Thursday but said 40 Saudi airstrikes hit Taiz, Marib and Hajjah in the previous 24 hours; that claim is unverified.

The Saudi-led coalition said it destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca before it entered prohibited airspace over the holy city; Houthi officials via their SABA agency denied targeting Mecca, and the two accounts are incompatible.

Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claims the Houthis shot down a Royal Saudi Air Force F-15 over Marib with a home-made missile; Saudi Arabia has not commented and no vetted outlet or independent imagery has confirmed it.

AFP-sourced reporting says at least 23 Yemeni government soldiers were killed in Houthi missile and drone attacks in two southwestern provinces over 24 hours, while 40 Houthi fighters were killed in Saudi airstrikes and ground fighting.

UN agencies via non-vetted outlets report roughly 112,000 people were displaced inside Yemen in the last two weeks, nearly 3,000 fled across the Gulf of Aden to Djibouti, and UNICEF says more than 57,000 of the displaced are children.

Saudi Civil Defence pushed mobile air-raid alerts just before 3 AM local time Saturday for Riyadh and nearby Al-Kharj, warning of a 'hostile aerial threat'; AFP and Reuters journalists in the capital reported hearing two explosions; the alert was lifted about 30 minutes later wit
These were the first air-raid alerts issued for Riyadh since the Houthis stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia in July.

Hours before the Riyadh alerts, a Houthi military spokesman said the group had foiled unspecified 'criminal attempts' in Sanaa, blamed Saudi Arabia, and threatened a response; Riyadh had not responded at report time.

The UN Security Council issued a statement Friday condemning 'in the strongest terms' continued Houthi attacks against Saudi Arabia, including attacks on civilian and energy infrastructure, and Houthi military escalation in Yemen.

US officials told CNN the United States has no plans for a counteroffensive against the Houthis despite their push toward Bab el-Mandeb; Washington's strategy is to rely on Saudi Arabia, though there are real doubts inside the US government that the Saudis can stop the Houthis al

CBS News reported, citing two sources, that Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman personally asked President Trump to take military action against the Houthis; the report has not been confirmed by a vetted outlet.
The Houthis claim Saudi Arabia launched 26 strikes on Houthi-held areas in the past 24 hours and about 300 over the past week; those counts are Houthi claims only, with no Saudi confirmation.
Yemen's Saudi-backed government says its forces killed 30 Houthi fighters and wounded more than 60 in clashes in Taiz's al-Wazi'iyah district.

WSJ (three officials): the Houthi strike apparently hit jet-fuel facilities at King Khalid International Airport; an AFP journalist on the ground saw firefighters tackling a burning Aramco-branded fuel tank at a depot near the airport; this is the first direct assault on Riyadh i

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree claimed two operations Saturday — 'sensitive' sites in Riyadh and an Aramco facility in Yanbu — using ballistic and cruise missiles plus drones, in retaliation for a Saudi attack on Sanaa.

Saudi-led coalition spokesman Col. Turki al-Malki said air defenses intercepted and destroyed a ballistic missile fired toward Riyadh early Saturday, and that attacks targeting civilians and infrastructure were thwarted in Bish/Baish, Taif, Farasan and Yanbu; he gave no damage de

A Reuters video Saturday night showed a massive plume of black smoke near Riyadh's main international airport, Saudi Arabia confirmed its air defenses intercepted a ballistic missile fired toward Riyadh at dawn, and the Saudi-led coalition said it foiled other Houthi attacks on t
Trump said his administration remains in contact with the Houthis and is avoiding direct U.S. military involvement in the group's conflict with Saudi Arabia.
Beijing privately asked Tehran to rein in the Houthis after a Saudi appeal, per Reuters sources cited September 17; Tehran answered that stability depends on ending the U.S.-Israeli war on Iran.

The Trump administration had prepared on Sunday to launch airstrikes against the Houthis in Yemen after fresh pleas from Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, but Trump called off the strikes at the last minute even as troops were loading bombs onto aircraft.

Trump spoke by phone Sunday with Rashad al-Alimi, president of Yemen's Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government, who asked for U.S. military help against the Houthis; two of the four sources said Trump made no direct pledge of support during the call.
Houthi fighters pushed on Monday to seize strategic highlands in Yemen in an effort to cut off the Red Sea coast from areas still held by Saudi-backed forces.

Yemen's government said Monday its forces struck Houthi fighters and supply lines in the Bab el-Mandeb area and Bayda province and claimed to have gone on the offensive, but heavy Houthi and local-tribal resistance continues and the government still holds the critical Taiz–Aden r

Houthi spokesman Yahya Saree claimed Saudi Arabia carried out 157 aircraft and missile strikes across four Yemeni provinces on Monday, bringing the total to 917 since the latest escalation began, and vowed a response; CNN could not independently verify the numbers and Saudi autho
The United Nations says nearly 700 people have been killed and thousands injured in the flare-up of fighting in Yemen, and more than 120,000 Yemenis have fled their homes within Yemen.

stories.title: BRICS New Delhi summit and declaration

claims.text: BRICS leaders unanimously adopted the New Delhi Declaration, expressing deep concern over Middle East escalation and urging maximum restraint through dialogue and diplomacy, without naming any country.
On the BRICS summit sidelines, Pezeshkian met Abu Dhabi Crown Prince Sheikh Khaled bin Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan, a notable direct Iran-UAE contact despite opposing sides in the war.

stories.title: Oil price shock (Brent above $100)

claims.text: Brent settled Friday at $104.61/bbl (down 2.8% on the day, up 8.7% on the week); WTI fell to $100.05 (up 9.4% on the week), with the pullback aided by reports of Oman's planned Hormuz meeting.

The U.S. national average diesel price topped $6 a gallon for the first time ever on Thursday, and the EIA estimated Middle East crude-production shut-ins averaged 6.7 million barrels a day in August.
Brent crude settled Friday at $104.61 a barrel, up 8.7% on the week, after spiking to $107.63 on Thursday; markets were closed Sunday.
Asked about the pipeline closure and moving marine traffic through the strait, President Trump said everything will 'work out fine.'
Brent crude jumped $3.62 (3.46%) at the market open to $108.23 a barrel; WTI rose $3.15 to $103.20 as of 22:14 GMT Sunday.
The US retail diesel price rose Sunday to another all-time high above $6.20 a gallon.
Brent crude rose 2.9% to $107.68 a barrel in early European trading Monday; WTI gained 2.8% to $102.88, after Brent gained 8.7% and WTI 9.4% last week.
Brent traded around $107.44 overnight (+2.7%); UK natural gas rose 4.3% to 207p a therm, its highest level since December 2022.
Markets priced an ~90% chance the Fed raises rates by 25bp on Wednesday after a hot August inflation report.
Economists estimate each $10 on a barrel of crude adds 0.2pp to inflation and trims growth by 0.1pp.
Brent settled Monday up 1% at $105.68 a barrel and WTI up 1.3% at $101.39, well off earlier intraday highs of $109.80 and $104.35.

Prices pulled back after Trump posted on Truth Social on Monday that Ukraine and Russia had agreed to stop attacking each other's energy infrastructure — though neither country independently confirmed any such deal, per Mizuho analyst Robert Yawger.

The Fed announces its policy decision at 2 p.m. ET Wednesday; markets are betting heavily on a quarter-point hike to a 3.75%-4.00% range — the first under Chairman Kevin Warsh — driven by elevated inflation and $100-a-barrel oil.

Economists now expect at least one more Fed hike to follow, with crude futures well above $100 and diesel at record highs 'amid the unremitting Middle East war' pushing inflation expectations sharply higher.

A hike would put Warsh, who started in May with Trump's expectation that he would cut rates, in a tight political spot weeks before the midterms; Trump has so far blamed 'political' fellow central bankers rather than Warsh himself.

Brent crude rose 1.8% to $107.59 a barrel and WTI gained 1.9% to $103.30 in early Tuesday European trading — above Monday's settlements ($105.68 / $101.39) but below Monday's intraday highs ($109.80 / $104.35).
US diesel hit a fresh record $6.27 a gallon on Tuesday, per AAA.
US oil executives warned a 'global fuel crisis has arrived' as commercial fuel stocks deplete and strategic reserves run low.

Saudi Arabia's TASI fell 0.8% in early Tuesday trade (Al Rajhi Bank -0.8%, Saudi Aramco -0.5%); Dubai's DFMGI and Abu Dhabi's FTFADGI each fell 0.2%, and Qatar's QSI fell 0.3% — on the fresh Houthi assault and the Hormuz shipping slump.
Commonwealth Bank's Vivek Dhar says global crude and product inventories give only five to eleven weeks of cover.
China's crude imports are edging higher.
Brent closed +2.9% at $108.75 and WTI +4.4% at $105.83 — the highest closes since May 19.

Libya's NOC said Tuesday operations are suspended at the Hamada and Tahara fields and a pumping station after the Petroleum Facilities Guard closed a valve on the main Hamada-Zawiya pipeline; the NOC may declare force majeure.
Libya volumes are small (~10,000 b/d per Argus), but the Guard threatens a partial cut for one week at Wafa, Al-Khamsa and El Feel, then a complete shutdown.
China's yuan-denominated Shanghai crude futures hit 929.4 yuan ($138.50)/bbl — a record since the contract's 2018 launch — driven by the Saudi pipeline outage and Chinese refiner buying.
Brent crude broke past $110 a barrel in September 16 Asian and European trading, up about 6% since the previous close, driven by the Saudi East-West pipeline outage and suspended loadings at Yanbu.
Brent pulled back to about $107.72 and WTI to about $104.28 by early September 16 after data showed an unexpectedly large build in US crude inventories.
Markets priced about a 93% chance that the Federal Reserve would raise rates by a quarter point to 3.75%-4.00% at its September 16 decision, the first hike since 2023.
The 10-year Treasury yield breached 5%, the S&P 500 was down 1.3% month-to-date, and August inflation ran 3.4% ahead of the September 16 Fed decision.
The Federal Open Market Committee voted unanimously, 12-0, to raise the benchmark rate by a quarter point to 3.75%-4%, the first rate hike since 2023, under newly confirmed Chair Kevin Warsh.
Chair Warsh said inflation is too high and has been for too long, with war-driven energy prices a key driver.
The Dow fell 631 points and the 10-year Treasury yield closed just above 5% for the first time in 19 years after the Fed's rate hike.
Brent crude fell 2.7% to $105.83 after the Fed hike on expectations higher rates will cool demand.
Chair Warsh declined to submit economic projections and acknowledged the Fed cannot affect individual prices such as gasoline.
The Fed's quarter-point hike defied President Trump's public demands for rate cuts, setting up a White House-Fed collision.
Saudi Arabia is reportedly offering extra crude cargoes through Oman, easing supply fears that had driven prices toward $110.
Brent fell $1.24 (about 1.2%) to $104.59 a barrel in early Thursday trade, after hovering near $108 on Wednesday.
US crude (WTI) was down to $101.29 in early Thursday trade.
The average US retail diesel price hit a new all-time high above $6.30 a gallon on Wednesday.
Brent fell for a second day, settling near $104.82 on Thursday.
Brent crude fell 2.6% to about $102.14 and WTI slipped below $100 ($99.53) in early European trading Friday, a third straight daily decline, on track for a weekly loss of nearly 2%.
MUFG's Soojin Kim said continued threats to both the Hormuz and Red Sea routes should keep Brent above pre-war levels, with volatility elevated.
Brent settled at $103.87 and WTI at $100.30 on Friday, as alternate exports and expected partial pipeline repairs outweighed escalation fears from Hormuz and the Red Sea.
Front-month ICE Brent settled at $103.87 on Friday, a third straight down session and the lowest settlement since September 9.
Brent fell for a fourth consecutive session on Monday, down 1.9% at $101.94 a barrel, and WTI fell 2% to $98.27, as improved Hormuz flows and UNGA diplomacy prospects eased supply fears.

Brent crude held near $100 a barrel through Monday, its lowest since early September, even as two tankers were hit in Hormuz and Yemen fighting escalated, with traders betting on the New York diplomatic window.
Brent crude fell 2.6% to $97.76 a barrel and WTI declined 3.1% to $92.78 on Tuesday after the Kyodo report landed, reversing an early rally that had taken Brent above $102.
Earlier Tuesday, Brent had risen 1.6% to $101.99 and WTI 1.7% to $97.40 on fading optimism about U.S.-Iran talks at the UN General Assembly, before the Kyodo report flipped the market.
Brent fell below $100 to ~$99.33 (down ~1%) and WTI settled near $94.80 — a fifth straight day of declines — whipsawing through the UN speech after the morning's Hormuz-offer plunge.

Trump said he backs the idea of a ban on diesel exports — 'I've said let's not send out the diesel' — during his UNGA press availability with Zelenskyy, with a decision coming 'fast, one way or the other'; Treasury Secretary Bessent said the administration is studying full versus
U.S. diesel sits at record highs (~$6.53/gal per AAA), with the Iran war cited as a price driver; Energy Secretary Wright warned a diesel-export ban would cut gasoline production.
Brent fell to $99.18 and WTI to $90.17 on Sept 23, a sixth straight daily decline — Brent's longest losing streak in over a year and its first sub-$100 close since September 8.

Saudi Arabia restarted its East-West pipeline to the Red Sea on Tuesday (rerouting ~4 million bpd to Yanbu), Iraq is exporting over 3 million bpd and expects to boost Turkey-route exports above 600,000 bpd, and U.S. crude inventories unexpectedly rose 1.8 million barrels.

stories.title: Ship attacks in the Strait of Hormuz

claims.text: An Iranian commercial vessel was struck near Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz overnight, killing one member of its ten-person crew and wounding several others, Iranian state media said.
The governor of Qeshm blamed a 'terrorist enemy' for the ship attack and said authorities had not yet identified the projectile; the U.S. military had not commented.
The UK Maritime Trade Operations centre said a second vessel was hit by an unknown projectile in the Strait of Hormuz late Saturday; a fire broke out and local authorities were evacuating the crew.

India's Ministry of External Affairs said the Panamanian-flagged MT El Gaia, carrying 14 Indians, was attacked off the Omani coast on Sunday; 13 have been rescued and search operations continue for one missing crew member.
US Central Command said on social media that American forces have redirected 100 commercial vessels through the strait over the past 60 days since the naval blockade of Iranian ports began.
Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz remains roughly 90% below pre-conflict levels.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps, via state-run Fars news agency on Monday, claimed the Panamanian-flagged tanker El Gaia hit sea mines while passing through a prohibited zone south of the Strait of Hormuz; US Central Command immediately called the claim false.

CENTCOM said the El Gaia was 'struck by an Iranian missile last month and rendered inoperable,' then struck again by an Iranian drone over the weekend — an account the IRGC directly contradicts with its sea-mine claim.
The UN's International Maritime Organization reported the El Gaia was damaged Saturday and that two seafarers were missing.

India's Ministry of External Affairs says 13 of the 14 Indian crew were rescued off the Omani coast and one remains missing, and condemned the attack — but the IMO reports two missing, so casualty counts are unconfirmed and contested.
CENTCOM said the El Gaia is now being towed by a regional partner.

ISW's September 14 assessment called the IRGC's mine claim false, said recent US strikes degraded Iranian coastal radars, surveillance, and mine-laying capabilities, and noted Tasnim acknowledging Iran's grip on the strait may be waning — analysis, not outlet-verified fact.

Axios reports the US military and Gulf nations have begun escorting tankers through Hormuz in daylight — the first daytime escorts since the short-lived Operation Project Freedom in May. Axios is not on the approved list; treat as reported, partially corroborated.
TankerTrackers satellite imagery shows large tankers transiting in and out in daylight, corroborating the escort reports.

Transit volumes are disputed: TankerTrackers' 60-day average crude flow is only ~7.85M bpd — well under Trump's 17M bpd claim — and Reuters/Kpler data over the weekend showed fewer than 10 transits a day. Mark volumes medium confidence.
The El Gaia dispute stands unchanged: the IRGC says mines, CENTCOM says Iranian missiles and drones, the maritime authority stays neutral.
An AIS-based challenge to the CENTCOM El Gaia account appeared on globalsecurity.org's imagery digest — unverified, low confidence.
US and Gulf partners continued daytime tanker escorts through the Strait of Hormuz, according to Axios.
TankerTrackers puts the 60-day average crude flow through the Strait of Hormuz at about 7.85 million barrels a day, well under the 17 million the US president has claimed.

Iran's Revolutionary Guard claims it intercepted the Togo-flagged tanker Trend in the Strait of Hormuz after an 'illegal attempt' to transit, warning unauthorized vessels would face 'destruction'; the AP could not independently confirm the claim.

UKMTO reported two separate incidents overnight: a security incident 16 nautical miles northeast of Khasab, Oman (crew safe, no environmental impact), and a tanker hit by an unknown projectile whose fire was later extinguished; AP could not verify whether the Trend is involved in
US-facilitated transits off Oman averaged 24 per day over the past week, but total Hormuz traffic remains roughly 90% below pre-war levels.

The International Maritime Organization has verified 80 attacks on merchant vessels in and around the Strait of Hormuz since February 28, and the head of the International Chamber of Shipping briefed the UN Security Council on September 18.

CENTCOM commander Adm. Brad Cooper said the U.S. military supported the transit of 1 billion barrels of oil through the Strait of Hormuz over the past two months; claimed Iran has 'exported zero barrels' because of the U.S. blockade; said the strait's primary transit lanes have b

Iran's armed forces spokesman Gen. Abolfazl Shekarchi called Cooper's figures 'false and ridiculous' and a 'failed psychological operation,' claiming the initiative in the strait remains in the hands of Iran's armed forces; no vetted outlet has verified either side's numbers.
UKMTO reported Monday that a tanker sailing into the Strait of Hormuz was struck by an unknown projectile, leaving two crew members with minor injuries.
UKMTO reported a second tanker was hit by debris in the Strait of Hormuz on Monday.

Neither of Monday's two Strait of Hormuz tanker incidents has been attributed to any group; they follow earlier strikes this month in the strait, including two supertankers carrying Saudi crude hit by unknown projectiles.

Reuters identified the two recently attacked tankers: the Isle of Man-flagged crude tanker LR Stephanie, managed by Universal Tanker Corp., was struck by an unidentified projectile entering the strait on Monday, injuring two crew members; the Liberia-flagged LPG tanker Al Maryah,
CENTCOM said the volume of oil, natural gas and cargo passing through the Strait of Hormuz over the past two weeks reached its highest level in six months, per the Wall Street Journal.

Three commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday (all exiting, including one Panamax tanker), down from 4 Monday and below the 10-day average of ~15, per Kpler data; LNG tanker Al Mafyar reappeared inside the strait after being last seen outside since Sept 19.

stories.title: Trump's Iran war endgame remarks

claims.text: Trump said the United States could 'stay in Iran and keep the oil,' drawing a parallel with the US deal in Venezuela, and claimed Venezuela's revenue had 'paid for the war many times.'
Trump repeated that he expects the Iran war to end this year, possibly just after the November midterm elections, and that gasoline prices would 'drop like a rock' once it does.
Trump added that Iran was 'calling constantly' for peace talks, an assertion Tehran has dismissed in the past.
Trump said Monday that oil is flowing through the Strait of Hormuz and that Iran 'wants to make a deal, quickly and badly.'
Trump posted Monday: 'Oil will drop like a rock as soon as the Military Conflict with Iran is over, and that will not be long.'
Trump said Wednesday evening he hopes the war is 'towards the end,' adding that Iran 'wants to make a deal' and that he had heard from Iran 'directly,' without elaborating.

Axios reported Trump is expected to meet leaders or foreign ministers of the six Gulf Cooperation Council states on the UN General Assembly sidelines on Tuesday, September 22; neither the State Department nor the White House confirmed it.
Trump told Axios's Barak Ravid he has a 'big decision' coming on Iran: 'Do I want to go in and annihilate them [the Iranian regime] or do I not? It's a big decision. Anything could happen with me.'
Trump said he wants to use Tuesday's expected meeting with Gulf Cooperation Council leaders at the UN General Assembly to gauge their positions before deciding his next steps.
Trump rebuffed Saudi pleas for direct American military intervention against the Houthis.
High US gasoline prices and low approval ratings make the Iran war a midterm-elections liability for Trump, per Reuters analysis.

In a ~37-minute UNGA address, Trump said he has 'a big decision to make': make a deal, or 'annihilate the Islamic Republic... quickly'; he called on all nations to join the 'total economic isolation of Iran,' accused Tehran of stalling a Hormuz deal until after the November 3 U.S
Most of Iran's lower-level delegation walked out of the UNGA hall about 10 minutes into Trump's speech (Pezeshkian and Araghchi were not in the hall); Cuba's delegation walked out too.
Secretary of State Rubio said Tuesday on Fox News that Trump 'is open to a meeting with him or anybody,' including Pezeshkian.

Trump told Middle East leaders about restoring Hormuz shipping: 'We think that the situation with Iran could end right after the (November 3) midterm elections, maybe before. I don't know. You never know.'

stories.title: Iran's 77-vessel Hormuz shipping blacklist

claims.text: Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority published an updated list Monday of 77 vessels it says are 'violating Iranian protocols for the Strait of Hormuz.'
Listed vessels face restrictions on future passage including fines, detention, or confiscation; vessels cooperating with the authority will also be added to the list.
The Strait Authority warned insurers, P&I clubs, and classification societies to stop providing services to the listed vessels; the list was posted on X.

Commodity vessel transits through the Strait of Hormuz fell to single-digit daily numbers over the weekend, vs a 10-day average of 14; four vessels exited the Gulf and ten entered, excluding ships running with AIS transponders switched off.
In the Bab el-Mandeb strait, 24 and 27 commodity vessels transited Saturday and Sunday respectively, vs a 10-day average of about 27.

The IRGC's maritime arm warned insurers, P&I clubs and classification societies on social media against servicing 'violating' vessels — an Iranian official claim with no approved-outlet pickup; unconfirmed.
Lloyd's List Intelligence, via TankerTrackers, reported only about 5 transits through the Strait of Hormuz on September 16, far below normal; no news outlet has verified the figure.
Only 3 commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz on Wednesday, down from 12 on Tuesday and far below the roughly 17-a-day average, per Kpler data published Thursday.

Saudi Arabia is boosting crude exports through the Strait of Hormuz itself via ship-to-ship transfers off Oman's Sohar port; Gulf of Oman STS volumes hit 2.7 million barrels per day versus 1.5 million in August.
The UAE's Adnoc is running ship-to-ship shuttle convoys through the Strait of Hormuz under US military protection, transferring crude to tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman.
Saudi Arabia diverted export volumes back to its Ras Tanura terminal on the Gulf coast and is loading tankers willing to brave the Strait of Hormuz.

Trade publication DeepDraft counted three separate Hormuz tanker incidents since September 16; Aramco sold about 60 million barrels of Ras Tanura crude for September/October loadings (~1-1.5 mbpd), some via ship-to-ship transfers near Sohar; VLCC day rates hit $870,947.

A dozen commodity vessels transited the Strait of Hormuz over the weekend, down from 35 the prior weekend, per provisional Kpler data cited by Reuters; Middle Eastern producers continue exporting on tankers travelling with transponders off.

Saudi Aramco is loading more crude at its Persian Gulf terminals, moving it through Hormuz, and transferring cargoes ship-to-ship off Oman, telling several Asian customers to pick up shipments off Oman; Gulf of Oman ship-to-ship activity has surged to record levels, per Kpler cit

Commodity vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell to two on Monday from 10 a day earlier, per preliminary Kpler data cited by Reuters; the strait typically handled about 125 large commercial vessels a day before the war.

stories.title: Report: Chinese entities supplied Iran satellite imagery before July Jordan base attack

claims.text: The Wall Street Journal reported that Iran acquired satellite imagery of a US base in Jordan from Chinese entities before a July attack there that killed three American troops.
The Journal cited unnamed US officials who declined to identify the Chinese entities and did not allege direct involvement by Beijing; Reuters could not independently verify the report.

Trump dismissed the report aboard Air Force One: 'They basically do what we do... When they say China spies on us, I say you're right and we spy on them too'; he did not say whether he would raise it with Xi Jinping.
Trump and Xi Jinping are expected to meet in the US on September 24, though China has not confirmed; Trump said Xi had 'behaved reasonably well.'
The July 17 ballistic-missile strike on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base in Jordan killed three US soldiers and wounded four who were evacuated.

ISW's September 18 China-Taiwan Update assesses 'PRC entities likely linked to the PLA' supplied the satellite imagery Iran used around the Jordan strike; the PLA link is ISW's assessment, not a US official allegation of direct Beijing involvement.
Wang Yi met Araghchi on September 16, urging Iran to limit the spread of the conflict and possibly pressing restraint on Houthi activity at Saudi Arabia's request.

stories.title: Pentagon watchdog's first accounting of Iran-war losses

claims.text: The Defense Department Inspector General released a special report Monday, the first formal accounting of US equipment and facility losses in the Iran war, covering February 28 through June 30.

Iranian strikes 'damaged and destroyed hundreds of buildings and structures' at US bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan, and depleted key US munition stockpiles.
Army medevac helicopters were withdrawn from Iraq and Kuwait, so 'most medical evacuations have been carried out by ground ... to local treatment facilities.'

The Navy's regional hub in Bahrain was destroyed — acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao said Iran 'blew the hell out of' it — forcing Diego Garcia to become the sea logistics hub and stretching resupply cycles to 14-18 days.

Damage to US diplomatic facilities totaled roughly $184 million; early-March Iranian drones hit the US Embassy in Riyadh (including the CIA station) and the Dubai consulate, and the Kuwait embassy suspended operations in March, resuming only emergency operations in late June.
More than 600 attacks on US facilities in Iraq caused the costliest damage of the war, about $157 million.

Up to 3,500 diplomatic personnel were out of the region between February 23 and June 30; most posts remain on 'restricted operations,' and officials have quietly discussed lasting post-war cuts to US personnel and facilities in the region.

CBS News published newly obtained photos of the aftermath of the March 2026 Iranian missile/drone strikes: the severed tail and destroyed radar dome of a USAF E-3 Sentry at Prince Sultan Air Base, destroyed trailers/barracks/vehicles at Camp Buehring, and building damage at Camp

The CBS photos document an earlier attack, not a new attack: they show the aftermath of the March 27 strikes. The underlying damage is already corroborated — CNN geolocated the E-3 wreckage to Prince Sultan; the Wall Street Journal and AP reported the March 27 strike (6 ballistic

A service member told CBS the damage 'hasn't been communicated to the American public' — unconfirmed, in tension with Monday's Pentagon inspector general loss accounting covered in this morning's edition.

stories.title: Container lines expand Red Sea/Suez transits despite Houthi grip

claims.text: Maersk said Monday that it and Gemini Cooperation partner Hapag-Lloyd will return four more services linking Asia, the Mediterranean and Europe to the Suez route, joining two returned earlier this year — even as the Houthis tightened control of the Bab el-Mandeb chokepoint.
MSC resumed some Red Sea transits last month; Cosco and OOCL are also returning, per Linerlytica data; CMA CGM began resuming late last year; Maersk says it will 'closely monitor' security.
UKMTO reported no new Red Sea shipping attacks in the week since the Houthi island capture, but rated the southern Red Sea threat as 'substantial' with northbound and southbound transits down.
At the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, 26 vessels crossed on Monday, unchanged from a day earlier, per Reuters citing shipping data.

stories.title: UN fact-finding mission warns Iran airstrikes may breach IHL

claims.text: The UN Human Rights Council fact-finding mission on Iran said 'repeated airstrikes causing civilian casualties raise serious questions' about international humanitarian law compliance, warning that failure to cease 'may give rise to international responsibility, including for war

The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran found reasonable grounds to believe the United States committed war crimes in two February strikes — on a primary school in Minab and a sports centre in Lamerd — with the report going to the UN Human Rights Council in Gen
The UN mission says more than 150 people were killed in the Shajareh Tayyebeh Primary School strike in Minab, including around 120 schoolchildren, per Iranian officials cited in the report.

The UN mission found the US relied on unverified intelligence about a senior Iranian commander and struck the Minab school while aware of a substantial risk of hitting a civilian object, conduct it says went beyond mere negligence.
The UN mission says a strike on a sports centre in Lamerd killed and injured 22 civilians and damaged nearby homes and a school, constituting an indiscriminate attack and therefore a war crime.
US Central Command said in March that US forces launched no strikes on the city of Lamerd that day, putting CENTCOM directly at odds with the UN mission's finding.

The same UN report found Iranian authorities committed crimes against humanity in the December-to-January protest crackdown — unlawful killings, torture, arbitrary detention and enforced disappearances — with a death toll likely far higher than the official figure of 3,038.
The Pentagon elevated its probe into the Minab strike but has published no preliminary findings.

White House spokeswoman Anna Kelly called the UN fact-finding mission's report 'unserious nonsense,' said the UN Human Rights Council has 'accomplished nothing for human rights,' and added that 'Iran is the only party in this conflict that has committed war crimes.'
The Pentagon declined to comment on the UN report, saying its investigation into the Minab strike remains ongoing.
The fact-finding mission is expected to present its findings to the 47-member UN Human Rights Council in Geneva on Monday.

At least 156 people, including 120 children and 26 teachers, were killed when the Shajareh Tayyiba school in Minab was struck on February 28, per Iranian officials — one of the worst civilian-casualty incidents in recent US military history.

CENTCOM built the Minab target coordinates using outdated Defense Intelligence Agency information: 2013 imagery showed the school and the IRGC naval base as one compound, a 2016 fence and separate entrance were missed, and December 2025 imagery showed children playing in the cour

The UN mission said 'no information indicates that the school was used for military purposes at the time,' and that the US failed its obligation to do everything feasible to verify the Minab school was a military objective.

CNN previously reported that senior US military commanders bypassed warnings in critical databases that intelligence on Iranian targets was severely out of date, and approved the February strikes anyway.

The Pentagon's internal investigation into the Minab strike stalled for months: the first two stages were completed within a week, confirming the strike hit the school and the US was responsible, but the third-stage DIA review 'has not yet been ordered,' and a separate CENTCOM in
A State Department official told CNN the administration 'did not find the report credible,' citing Trump's February 2025 withdrawal from the UN Human Rights Council.

The UN's Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Iran presented its report — finding 'reasonable grounds' to believe the U.S. committed war crimes in the Minab and Lamerd strikes, and that Iran committed crimes against humanity in its protest crackdown — to the Human Ri

Washington says it does 'not give credibility' to the UN fact-finding mission's findings, the White House called the council's work unserious and insisted Iran is the only party guilty of war crimes, while Tehran denied investigators access to the country and left roughly three d

stories.title: US blocks Iran nuclear chief's travel to IAEA meeting

claims.text: The US blocked a snapback-sanctions travel exemption for Iran's nuclear chief Mohammad Eslami, so Austria revoked his visa and he missed the IAEA General Conference in Vienna; Iran and Russia protested.

stories.title: Iran limiting access to Pickaxe Mountain tunnel entrances

claims.text: The Institute for Science and International Security published Sept 14 satellite imagery saying Iran is limiting access to tunnel entrances at Pickaxe Mountain — credible analysts, but no approved-outlet pickup; unconfirmed.

Analytic shops (ISIS/ISW) claim September 17 satellite imagery shows Iran rapidly rebuilding the Taleghan 2 facility at Parchin and hardening Natanz and the 'Pickaxe Mountain' site; no vetted outlet has confirmed.

stories.title: US destroys two Iranian boats in drone clash off Larak Island

claims.text: CENTCOM spokesman Capt. Tim Hawkins said the US destroyed two small Iranian boats this week that were trying to take possession of a US unmanned surface vessel off Iran, identifying the drone as a roughly 25-foot Saildrone and saying all surface drones 'remain fully accounted for

Iranian state media (IRNA), citing Hormozgan deputy governor Ahmad Nafisi, said Monday evening a pair of fishing boats off the Kargan coast near Larak Island came under attack from an 'enemy drone' and several fishermen are missing, with search and rescue underway; the Iranian ac
Axios, citing an anonymous US official, says two missiles were fired and most of those on board were killed — unconfirmed; no approved outlet has corroborated the casualty claim.

The identity of the boats and the casualties are contested: the US says an attempted drone theft by the Guard; Iran says fishermen under attack. The AP verified the CENTCOM statement itself, so a clash happened, but neither side's boat-identity or casualty version is verified.

The Fifth Fleet said the two boats destroyed off Larak Island were IRGC Navy craft destroyed in international waters while attempting to seize a US Navy Saildrone, with all US surface drones accounted for and no Americans hurt.

Iran's Mehr News Agency, quoting Hormozgan deputy governor Ahmad Nafisi, said two fishing boats were hit by an enemy drone off the Kargan coast near Larak Island on Monday night, with several fishermen still missing three days later and search and rescue underway.

stories.title: MBS holds one-day Cairo visit; Red Sea navigation tops agenda

claims.text: Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman made a one-day working visit to Cairo, meeting President Sisi at Al-Ittihadiya Palace, followed by expanded delegation talks (Saudi delegation included FM Prince Faisal bin Farhan) and a luncheon; he departed the same day.

The Egyptian presidency readout: both leaders stressed freedom and security of navigation in the Bab el-Mandeb Strait and the Red Sea; Sisi backed Saudi measures to protect its security and stability and called for a comprehensive, sustainable political solution to the Yemen cris
Neither side gave firm details on any future steps; Egypt is unlikely to offer military help — mark remaining questions unconfirmed.

stories.title: US strikes on suspected drug boats in the Caribbean; Trump links campaign to Iran

claims.text: Trump announced on September 15 that the US military carried out a lethal kinetic strike on a suspected drug boat in the Southern Command area of responsibility, killing the three people aboard with no US forces harmed.
The September 15 Caribbean strike was at least the third such US strike on suspected drug boats this month.

Trump said the targeted vessel was affiliated with a designated terrorist organization and was trafficking narcotics toward the United States, but the administration provided no evidence the boat was carrying drugs and did not identify who was aboard.
Trump said the Caribbean strike was a separate operation from the Gulf boat clash off Larak Island.
Trump posted on Truth Social that Iran and Venezuela are working together, offering no evidence; no news outlet has corroborated the claim.
Senators from both parties and human rights groups questioned the legality of using military force for at-sea law enforcement without congressional authorization.

stories.title: IRGC Navy units observed escorting dark-fleet tankers off Kish Island

claims.text: TankerTrackers observed IRGC naval units about 14 nautical miles off Kish Island escorting dark-fleet tankers moving sanctioned oil; no news outlet has verified the observation.

stories.title: Russia and China veto extension of Iran sanctions monitoring

claims.text: Russia and China vetoed a UN Security Council resolution that would have extended the mandate for independent monitoring of international sanctions on Iran; eleven council members voted in favor and Pakistan and Somalia abstained.

Deputy US Ambassador Jennifer Locetta told the Security Council that without an independent panel of experts, 'this council loses its principal source of impartial, evidence-based reporting on sanctions violations.'

UN sanctions on Iran were reimposed a year ago after France, Britain and Germany accused Tehran of violating the 2015 nuclear deal; Russia and China revived the argument Thursday that all UN measures on Tehran had been removed under that deal.

stories.title: UNGA High-Level Week: Iran's leaders granted US visas

claims.text: The State Department approved visas Thursday for Iran's core UNGA delegation, including President Masoud Pezeshkian and Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi; the delegation faces travel restrictions and bans on luxury-goods purchases and is smaller than last year's.
Pezeshkian is expected to address the UN General Assembly on Wednesday, his first visit to the United States since the war began on February 28.
The Iran visa approvals came a day after the US denied visas to Palestinian Authority and PLO delegations for the second year running.
Most European and Asian allies have spurned Trump's demands for assistance in the Iran war effort.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi departed Tehran on Sunday evening for the UN General Assembly in New York with a stopover in Doha, where Qatar has acted as the go-between in the war, per Iranian state media reported by the AP.
President Pezeshkian will leave Tehran on Tuesday and address the UN General Assembly on Wednesday morning, his first appearance on U.S. soil since the war began, per IRNA.

The State Department says the visa approvals for Iran's scaled-down core delegation are consistent with American host-country obligations to the United Nations; the delegation faces tight travel limits and prohibitions on luxury-goods purchases.
Qatari officials plan to use the UNGA gathering to discuss resuming talks, multiple diplomats said, but no formal talks with Iran are confirmed.
UN Secretary-General António Guterres told reporters that serious U.S.-Iran dialogue 'probably will take place somewhere else,' not New York, managing down expectations for the General Assembly week.
Trump is set to address the General Assembly on Tuesday and Pezeshkian is expected to speak Wednesday; Trump did not rule out meeting Pezeshkian in New York.
Trump met Tuesday with leaders from Bahrain, Kuwait, Oman, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Jordan to discuss what the AP described as 'the way ahead with the war.'

stories.title: US approves $24.3B F-35 sale to Saudi Arabia

claims.text: The State Department approved a potential sale of 48 F-35A fighters and 49 engines to Saudi Arabia valued at $24.3 billion, opening a 30-day congressional review period during which Congress can block it.
Trump pledged the F-35 sale last year as part of what he called a Strategic Defense Agreement; the State Department notice claims the sale 'will not alter the military balance in the region.'
US intelligence warned the F-35 sale could give Beijing access to the jet's sensitive technology, and some lawmakers have raised concerns.

stories.title: International naval deployments respond to Red Sea threat

claims.text: Italian defence minister Guido Crosetto said Italy is preparing its own naval mission to protect merchant shipping through Bab el-Mandeb, declaring Italy 'cannot wait for the EU to respond.'

Crosetto said 'After what I said, something moved within Aspides, but we need more ships'; Italy and Greece are the only nations substantially supporting the EU escort effort, and Rome did not detail ships or measures for its own mission.
Reuters notes Bab el-Mandeb carries about 7% of global oil output and roughly 40% of Italy's external trade uses the Suez route.
South Korea is considering expanding its Cheonghae naval unit's operations in the Gulf of Aden to protect Korean shipping and oil routes, explicitly ruling out intervening in the war.

EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the Aspides mission raised the alert level of its vessels in the Red Sea and will reinforce coordination with the Saudi-led multinational maritime coalition; the statement has not been matched to a direct vetted-outlet page.

In a Friday interview, Italian defence minister Guido Crosetto said 'the only nations really supporting' the Red Sea security effort are Italy and Greece; Italy's shipowners association says about 40% of the country's trade with the rest of the world passes through the Suez route
Kpler data shows petroleum volumes transiting Bab el-Mandeb were about 7% of global oil output in June.

President Lee Jae Myung said Friday there will be no deployment of troops or military assets that would involve or draw Korea into wars; Cheonghae's protective role continues but combat participation is off the table.

stories.title: Hundreds of thousands rally in Tehran for the government

claims.text: AP reported hundreds of thousands of people attended Tehran's largest pro-government rally since the war began.

stories.title: U.S. embassy security alerts across the Middle East

claims.text: Four confirmed official September 19 security alerts — U.S. Embassy Iraq (Baghdad), U.S. Embassy Saudi Arabia, U.S. Embassy Manama, and U.S. Embassy Beirut — carry nearly identical boilerplate warning of Houthi hostilities against Saudi Arabia including civilian airports, potenti

Claims of same-day September 19 alerts at U.S. missions in Jerusalem, Muscat, Kuwait, Qatar, Jordan, Egypt and the UAE — carried by Iranian outlets and social media accounts — were not found on those missions' official sites as of the evening's checks; the wider wave is unverifie
None of the four confirmed September 19 alerts uses 'shelter in place' or 'leave immediately' language; they are vigilance and flight-disruption warnings, not evacuation orders.

The U.S. Embassy in Israel issued a security alert Saturday over escalated Houthi-Saudi fighting, and the U.S. virtual embassy in Iran issued a similar alert warning of rapid escalation and travel disruption.

The State Department's Saturday alert warned of the potential for rapid escalation across the Middle East and told Americans to exercise heightened vigilance and expect possible flight cancellations and airspace closures.
The U.S. Embassy in Saudi Arabia restricted U.S. government personnel travel to the cities of Taif and Yanbu without special authorization.

stories.title: Iran's three conditions for ending the war

claims.text: SNSC secretary Mohsen Rezaei told Al Jazeera that Tehran has conveyed three conditions to Washington through Qatari mediators: end the war on all fronts (explicitly including the Yemen and Saudi-Houthi fighting), release Iran's frozen and seized assets, and end the U.S. naval blo

Rezaei warned Iran is ready for a 'decisive war' if the demands are rejected; said Iran has not decided to withdraw from the NPT but that further pressure could change that; claimed an unverified test firing of an anti-ship missile near a U.S. aircraft carrier; and said Iran woul

Pakistan's foreign minister Ishaq Dar spoke by phone with Iranian FM Abbas Araghchi about uninterrupted energy supplies and safe passage for commercial ships; Pakistan cited the effects of disruptions on developing countries.
CENTCOM said on social media that as of September 20 its forces have redirected 109 commercial vessels to ensure compliance with the U.S. naval blockade of Iranian ports.
Tehran says it is still awaiting a U.S. response to the three conditions it conveyed through Qatari mediators, per the AP's September 21 reporting.

stories.title: Turkey-Saudi Arabia-Pakistan defense pact

claims.text: Turkish foreign minister Hakan Fidan told NTV that Turkey would face 'no difficulty in meeting' any military needs from Saudi Arabia under the recently signed Turkey-Saudi Arabia-Pakistan defense pact, and that 'we observe very serious attacks on Saudi Arabia's territorial integr
Asked directly, Fidan did not rule out the Turkey-Saudi Arabia-Pakistan alliance engaging in military action against the Houthis.

stories.title: Iran executes man convicted of spying for Mossad

claims.text: Iran state TV reported Hossein Pedram was executed after being convicted of sharing classified information on 'sensitive military sites' in Isfahan province with Israel's Mossad; he was reportedly arrested after those sites — including missile bases — were targeted in the 12-day

stories.title: Israeli strikes in Gaza and Lebanon

claims.text: Gaza's Health Ministry and Shifa Hospital report Israeli strikes Saturday killed one man in Shijaiyah, another in Jabaliya, and that a strike on a civilian vehicle in Gaza City killed one and wounded at least four; the Israeli military said it struck military operatives.

In southern Lebanon, the IDF said it struck Hezbollah targets across several areas after two soldiers were wounded when their vehicle drove over a Hezbollah explosive device in an area occupied by Israeli troops; Lebanon's national news agency reported three Israeli airstrikes on

stories.title: US-Iran threat exchange over a new American attack

claims.text: Iran's Khatam al-Anbiya Central Headquarters warned on state media Sunday that it had information the United States is preparing a major new attack, and that any fresh strike would trigger sustained retaliation against American bases and interests, with regional allies assisting

Trump told Fox News on September 20 that he is in 'deciding mode' on Iran, asking 'if and when do I blow the entire nation up,' saying 'very big things' could happen soon, listing three possible outcomes — a deal, economic pressure, or military action — while saying he remains op
There have been no publicly reported U.S. strikes on Iran for more than two weeks, per CNN's assessment, making the September 20 threat exchange more about pressure than imminent action.

Iran's Armed Forces issued a statement dismissing Trump's UNGA address as 'propaganda' and saying Tehran stands in 'full readiness to inflict more severe, crushing, and unpredictable blows on the aggressors.'

Iran's General Staff, quoted via the Mehr news agency, accused Trump of using the UN platform to justify 'aggression' and called the threats 'not a sign of power but a sign of their strategic desperation.'

stories.title: Dispute over the count of US war dead

claims.text: The Washington Post, citing six U.S. officials familiar with Pentagon internal casualty accounting, reported at least 22 U.S. service members have died since February 28 — four more than the 18 in the Pentagon's public database — with one official putting the figure at 23, and th

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth called the Washington Post casualty report 'a complete LIE,' 'DISGUSTING and FAKE,' and said the paper is 'worse than Iranian state media'; the Pentagon declined to answer the paper's questions about the discrepancy.

stories.title: Trump cuts Camp David stay short, returns to White House a day early

claims.text: Trump returned to the White House on Saturday evening, a day ahead of schedule, cutting his Camp David stay short; the White House gave no explanation, and no outlet has tied the early return to any single event.

stories.title: U.S. moves to ground Iranian airlines worldwide via secondary sanctions

claims.text: Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on CNBC Monday that 'On September 23, all the Iranian airlines will be shut down around the world,' warning that airports and companies providing fuel, landing services, or ticketing to Iranian carriers risk being cut off from the U.S. dollar

Iraq ordered its civil aviation authority to suspend Iranian flights to Baghdad airport starting Wednesday, two sources told Reuters, after the U.S. threatened to sanction airports servicing Iranian carriers; Baghdad is discussing diverting Iranian Airways flights to Najaf airpor

Tasnim, citing Iran's Civil Aviation Organization, said flights from Tehran to Baghdad and Muscat are canceled starting Wednesday while remaining international flights including Istanbul operate on schedule; the organization told ISNA that Iranian travelers are not currently bein
